problem: Camera-only navigation among moving humans is largely unexplored: prior crowd-navigation RL uses LiDAR or known human positions, image-based navigation work ignores dynamic humans, and existing 3D simulators lack multiple moving pedestrians.
motivation: Monocular cameras are cheap and ubiquitous and carry cues such as body motion that range sensors miss, but images are high-dimensional and hard for end-to-end RL. The authors' prior LiDAR work showed world-model features help crowd navigation, so they test whether this transfers to images.
key_idea: Pre-train a self-supervised (transformer/RSSM) world model to predict future images, use its latent features as input to a small PPO controller (or Dreamer-style dream training) for monocular crowd navigation, and provide an open-source photorealistic simulator (NavDreams) for sim2real.
insight: World-model latents are richer than end-to-end features: decoders on them get about half the per-pixel error for depth and segmentation, and the end-to-end features tend to lose pedestrians. World-model pretraining on more diverse data helps even on unseen scenarios, while generalist controllers trade seen-scene performance for unseen-scene generalization, so overfitting is a bigger problem for images than for LiDAR. Pixel-wise dream error does not track visual dream quality (the blurriest transformer with z=64 has the lowest error), and the choice of world-model architecture (RSSM, TSSM, transformer) does not change controller performance.
method: NavDreams simulator: open-source gym-compatible 3D simulator with 7 scenarios (simple, city, office, modern, cathedral, gallery, replica). Difficulty scales goal distance, number of humans and obstacles. Realism features include camera shake, inertia, lighting randomization and human behaviors.
Problem setup: 64x64 RGB image plus 2D goal vector, discrete actions [LEFT, FORWARD, RIGHT], sparse goal reward (100) or shaped reward with collision -25, progress and turn penalty.

World model W: CNN image encoder, FC encoders for action and vector, causal transformer predicting the next image and vector. Latent size 64, loss is MSE prediction + reconstruction + 0.001*KL. It takes continuous velocity actions so it can train on real robot logs. Variants trained on S, SC, SCR or R data; RSSM, TSSM and a z=1024 transformer are also tried.
Controller C (WM+PPO): MLP with two 1024 layers on the latest world-model latent z_t plus the goal vector, trained with PPO and a difficulty curriculum (+1 after success, -1 after failure).
End-to-end baseline: same encoder and MLP trained jointly with PPO from single-timestep observations.
WM+Dreamer: DreamerV2-style actor-critic trained on world-model dreams with on-policy world-model updates, trained on simple, modern and replica.
Sim2real: train the controller in the replica scene (randomized lighting and objects, camera-matched post-processing) and deploy on a Pepper robot.

setting.backbone: Transformer/RSSM/TSSM world model + MLP controller trained with PPO or Dreamer (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Simulator rollouts from a stochastic heuristic policy in simple/city/office/modern scenarios plus real-robot recordings for the world model; controllers trained online with PPO in the simulator (5M steps per controller)
setting.observation: monocular RGB 64x64 plus 2D relative goal vector
setting.action_space: discrete [LEFT, FORWARD, RIGHT] (converted to continuous velocity for the world model)
setting.privileged: none at test time (goal position in robot frame is given as input)

results: Controllers using world-model features outperform end-to-end PPO in every scenario and reach higher curriculum difficulty. Dreamer training beats WM+PPO (simple 82% vs 57%, modern 50% vs 30%). The replica policy reaches 94/55/17% success with 0/3/10 people in simulation and 66% (36/54) on a real Pepper robot.
limitations: Success drops sharply with crowd density (17% with 10 people in replica), and the images are only 64x64.
Controllers overfit to the training scenarios and generalist controllers lose seen-scene performance; the real-robot test is small, in one environment.
Dreamer training is very compute heavy (over 1 week per model) and was run on only three scenarios; the policy remains short-sighted and planning is weak.
